{"id": "20:10/q23", "question": "How does this telling relate to other tellings of Moses' fire?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "20:10/q23/p1", "position": "Parallel passages vary their wording while recounting the same episode.", "reasons": "Al-Bāqillānī cites Ṭā Hā, al-Naml and al-Qaṣaṣ as varied expression that broadens the challenge to produce comparable discourse, citing 27:8, 28:29 and 52:34; he says paraphrase reveals the loss of Qurʾānic wording. {"id": "20:10/q24", "question": "How does the episode serve the surrounding sūra?", "turns_on": "The sources emphasize consolation, literary and narrative sequence, or the beginning of the prophetic call.", "positions": [{"id": "20:10/q24/p1", "position": "It consoles Muhammad through Moses' trials and God's support.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabarī says the episode amid Quraysh's persecution promises Muhammad's eventual ascendancy and weakening of unbelievers' schemes, urging endurance in worship and effort. {"id": "20:10/q25", "question": "What inward meaning is given to the fire and Moses' hopes?", "turns_on": "Different inward readings identify the fire with the Holy Spirit, divine manifestation, or spiritual awakening.", "positions": [{"id": "20:10/q25/p1", "position": "The fire is the Holy Spirit illuminating souls, and the family are Moses' faculties.", "reasons": "Al-Qāshānī says the faculties remain still as sensory activity quiets; the firebrand is a luminous benefit to them, while finding a guide is gaining knowledge and gnosis leading to truth."}, {"id": "20:10/q25/p2", "position": "God appeared in the desired form of fire to draw Moses toward Him.", "reasons": "Bursevī transmits some Sufis' explanation that another form might have made Moses turn away; his poem says Moses did not yet recognize the divine manifestation in light and speech."}, {"id": "20:10/q25/p3", "position": "The fire symbolizes rising spiritual certainty.", "reasons": "The Study Quran adds the mountain of God, Horeb, from Exodus; Asad treats the lost road as a possible symbol of spiritual need and the fire as a burning-bush allegory."}]}
{"id": "20:10/q26", "question": "How did Moses recognize the divine call at the fire?", "turns_on": "Inference from the character of the speech versus direct divinely given recognition.", "positions": [{"id": "20:10/q26/p1", "position": "He inferred it from the speech's ordered structure and composition.", "reasons": "Al-Qushayrī says this recognition came when he tried to take a flame."}, {"id": "20:10/q26/p2", "position": "God made His speech known through special inspiration without inference.", "reasons": "Al-Qushayrī reports this alternative."}]}
{"id": "20:10/q27", "question": "Why did Moses remove his sandals, according to related reports?", "turns_on": "The reports appeal to the sandals' material, the valley's blessing, or symbolic humility.", "positions": [{"id": "20:10/q27/p1", "position": "They were made from donkey hide.", "reasons": "Al-Thaʿlabī transmits Ibn Masʿūd's report from the Prophet specifying a dead donkey and a variant specifying untanned hide; al-Ḥasan contrasts this with Muhammad's prayer in sandals."}, {"id": "20:10/q27/p2", "position": "His bare feet could touch and receive the blessed ground.", "reasons": "ʿIkrima and Mujāhid call it twice sanctified; another explanation singles out his heels."}, {"id": "20:10/q27/p3", "position": "Barefootedness expresses humility or detachment from family.", "reasons": "Al-Thaʿlabī reports these explanations, adding that shoes in dreams signify a wife."}, {"id": "20:10/q27/p4", "position": "Removing sandals was associated with the sacred valley.", "reasons": "Abū al-Aḥwaṣ reports Ibn Masʿūd joking to Abū Mūsā, who had removed sandals before prayer, 'Are you in the sacred valley?'"}]}
{"id": "20:10/q28", "question": "How are other nearby words and the preceding question explained?", "turns_on": "These are separate contextual observations included in the collected notes.", "positions": [{"id": "20:10/q28/p1", "position": "The preceding hal keeps its ordinary confirmatory interrogative sense.", "reasons": "Al-Samīn also reports proposed readings as qad or as negation."}, {"id": "20:10/q28/p2", "position": "Akhfaytu can mean concealed or revealed, while khafaytu means revealed only.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabrisī records the distinction and also glosses radā and taraddā as destruction."}, {"id": "20:10/q28/p3", "position": "Saʿy means swift movement or action, and radā and ardā concern perishing and destroying.", "reasons": "Abū Ḥayyān cites Durayd ibn al-Ṣimma's poetry for ardā."}, {"id": "20:10/q28/p4", "position": "The king's dream in Joseph was true inspiration, not the confused dreams claimed by his court.", "reasons": "Bint al-Shāṭiʾ cites 12:43–44 in her wider discussion of distinctive Qurʾānic diction."}]}

{"id": "21:18/q02", "question": "What does naqdhif convey?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "21:18/q02/p1", "position": "It means throwing or hurling truth forcefully against falsehood.", "reasons": "Wahidi and Bagawi give the basic sense; Raghib as cited by Bursevi and Alusi specifies a distant, forceful throw with hard impact. {"id": "21:18/q03", "question": "What are the truth and falsehood cast against each other?", "turns_on": "The notes variously identify the pair with revelation and lies, proof and claims, faith and shirk, seriousness and play, or unrestricted truth and falsehood.", "positions": [{"id": "21:18/q03/p1", "position": "The truth includes the Quran or God's revelation, and falsehood includes unbelievers' lies, denial or confusion.", "reasons": "Yahya, Tabari, Zajjaj, Wahidi, Ibn al-Jawzi, Biqai and Durr identify Quran or Book; Tabari specifies revelation against denial, Wahidi reports Abu Ishaq's Quran against lies, and Durr cites Qatada's confusion. Biqai stresses the Quran's firm argument and lack of frivolity."}, {"id": "21:18/q03/p2", "position": "Truth is broad, including Quran, message, law, faith and all truth; falsehood covers their opposites generally.", "reasons": "Ibn Atiyya names Quran, message and law; Abu Hayyan reports the same broad view; Bagawi calls truth faith; Tabataba'i takes the rule across belief, practice and creation; Alusi prefers the general reading over restriction to proof and claims about a child. {"id": "21:18/q04", "question": "What does yadmughuhu mean?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "21:18/q04/p1", "position": "It strikes the head or brain, a fatal blow, and thus destroys or defeats falsehood.", "reasons": "Ibn Qutayba, Tabari, Mawardi, Wahidi citing Ibn Qutayba, Bagawi, Ibn Atiyya, Samīn, Jishumi, Ibn al-Jawzi, Baydawi, Tabataba'i, Islahi and Study Quran cite the brain wound; Samīn compares verbs named for the struck body part. {"id": "21:18/q05", "question": "How does the casting and crushing image work?", "turns_on": "Alusi's distinction is between an explicit overall simile and a concealed comparison through the physical verbs.", "positions": [{"id": "21:18/q05/p1", "position": "It depicts strong truth as a hard projectile crushing weak, hollow falsehood, making abstract defeat vivid.", "reasons": "Kashshaf, Razi, Baydawi, Nasafi, Abu Hayyan, Biqai and Bursevi give the hard/soft image; Bursevi cites Sahib al-Miftah on physical words transferred to abstract realities; Burhan says both verbs are metaphors. Alusi prefers a full simile of thrown body and soft brain, with truth's height and falsehood's lowliness, to a hidden metaphor. Ibn Ashur says both images transfer physical action to thought. Abu Ishaq, cited by Wahidi, says the defeat makes falsehood disappear in abasement and humiliation. Rummani says the choice of qadhf pictures irresistible overpowering without doubt or hesitation, while damgh conveys a stronger, clearer impact than mere removal. Itqan explains that perceptible acts are borrowed for abstract truth and falsehood because of their shared relation."}, {"id": "21:18/q05/p2", "position": "The image may be a hidden metaphor comparing truth and falsehood to the two bodies.", "reasons": "Alusi states this alternative but prefers the full simile."}]}
{"id": "21:18/q06", "question": "How is fa-yadmaghuhu read and parsed?", "turns_on": "The final verb's case or mood and the possible source of the rare mim vowel.", "positions": [{"id": "21:18/q06/p1", "position": "The common reading raises the final ghayn, coordinating the imperfect verb.", "reasons": "Samīn calls this the common reading and its grammatical coordination; Sibawayh notes more generally that jussive inflection belongs to imperfect verbs and compares it to noun genitive."}, {"id": "21:18/q06/p2", "position": "Isa ibn Umar reads the final ghayn with accusative/subjunctive inflection.", "reasons": "Kashshaf calls it weak and cites a poetic subjunctive ending fa-astariha; Abu Hayyan and Samīn repeat that judgment. Baydawi parses by meaning or coordination with al-haqq and cites anonymous poetry. Alusi says fa does not govern it here; Abu al-Baqa coordinates it with al-haqq, while Alusi prefers coordination with the underlying sense of throwing then crushing. A proposed indicative with light emphatic nun in the poem is weak, making the verse reading weaker."}, {"id": "21:18/q06/p3", "position": "A rare reading puts a damma on the mim, and another transmits damma on mim and ghayn.", "reasons": "Abu Hayyan transmits the mim variant from Zamakhshari; Samīn explains it as dialect variation in the imperfect or assimilation from the guttural; Alusi reports both vowels raised."}]}
{"id": "21:18/q07", "question": "What does zahiq mean?", "turns_on": "Jishumi lists a separate lexical usage, while the contextual glosses agree on disappearance.", "positions": [{"id": "21:18/q07/p1", "position": "It is departing, vanishing or perishing.", "reasons": "Ibn Qutayba, Zajjaj, linguists cited by Nahhas, Qatada cited by Abd al-Razzaq, Tabari, Mawardi, Wahidi and Tabrisi, and later commentators give these near senses. {"id": "21:18/q14", "question": "How widely does the warning apply?", "turns_on": "Whether the specific address also states a standing rule for later false descriptions.", "positions": [{"id": "21:18/q14/p1", "position": "It extends to anyone making a false description until the Resurrection, including false claims about God's attributes or rulings.", "reasons": "Wahidi reports Hasan and applies it to attributes and rulings; Durr reports Hasan; Biqai extends it to descriptions of Quran, God and world made on whim without divine warrant because people lack full grasp of realities."}, {"id": "21:18/q14/p2", "position": "The warning specifically condemns the contemporary unbelievers' false assertions.", "reasons": "Wahidi and Bagawi describe their unfitting attribution; Alusi identifies the immediate addressees; Tabataba'i identifies deniers of resurrection and prophethood."}]}
{"id": "21:18/q15", "question": "What lasting relation between truth and falsehood does the verse teach?", "turns_on": "The notes distinguish an unrestricted metaphysical rule from the specific means of its enactment.", "positions": [{"id": "21:18/q15/p1", "position": "Truth has real stability and ultimately overcomes transient falsehood throughout belief, practice and creation.", "reasons": "Tabataba'i says falsehood only resembles truth, like mirage water; its deficiencies depend on a more complete reality and it exists by God's permission. He invokes 13:17, 24:25, 2:147 and 38:27, calls God absolute truth, and says the imperfect verb signals God's continuing practice. Kuranyolu says falsehood cannot remain in truth's presence; the Sadiq reports generalize the rule. Study Quran points to 17:81, 8:8, 34:49 and 42:24. Qashani's inward reading treats transient beings as perishing when God's essential disclosure reveals the falsity of their claimed independent existence, attributes, acts and effects."}, {"id": "21:18/q15/p2", "position": "God's truth overcomes falsehood through revealed proof, warning, destruction, discernment or force against wrongdoers.", "reasons": "Ibn Ashur enumerates these means and cites 8:12; Tabrisi says God who manifests truth by proofs cannot play falsehood; Ibn Kathir says He makes truth plain and erases falsehood."}]}
{"id": "21:18/q16", "question": "Why is falsehood given time before truth defeats it?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "21:18/q16/p1", "position": "Respite tests human choice and does not put good and evil on equal footing; God then makes truth prevail.", "reasons": "Islahi states the trial of those choosing truth or clinging to evil; Tabataba'i says God gives falsehood time but preserves true belief, perfection and prophetic victory despite few followers or strong opposition."}]}
{"id": "21:18/q17", "question": "What does the verse imply about human knowledge and freedom?", "turns_on": "These are two distinct doctrinal implications drawn by Jishumi, rather than rival readings.", "positions": [{"id": "21:18/q17/p1", "position": "It refutes necessary knowledge, since universal compulsion to know would leave no disagreement.", "reasons": "Jishumi argues that if knowledge were necessary everyone would form one community."}, {"id": "21:18/q17/p2", "position": "It refutes determinism, since sending prophets presupposes that people can move from unbelief to faith.", "reasons": "Jishumi draws this conclusion from prophetic missions."}]}

{"id": "21:18/q19", "question": "How does the verse connect to other passages and the sura's argument?", "turns_on": "The connections differ by neighboring argument versus verbal and thematic parallels elsewhere.", "positions": [{"id": "21:18/q19/p1", "position": "It follows the denial of purposeless creation and supports the surrounding argument for God's wisdom and oneness.", "reasons": "Islahi says a wise, just Creator will bring a day when truth wins; multiple independent gods would undo the universe, all prophets taught monotheism, and angels are servants rather than daughters or autonomous intercessors. {"id": "21:18/q20", "question": "What reports apply the truth's victory more broadly?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "21:18/q20/p1", "position": "Al-Sadiq is reported to say truth defeats falsehood whenever they meet, and reaches every person.", "reasons": "Yunus transmits the first report through al-Mahasin; Ayyub ibn al-Hurr transmits the second, saying truth breaks the heart of one who accepts or leaves it. {"id": "21:18/q21", "question": "What inward readings are drawn from truth overcoming falsehood?", "turns_on": "The degree of inward defeat: moral acts, attributes, or all created selfhood.", "positions": [{"id": "21:18/q21/p1", "position": "Admonition or divine command defeats sin and forbidden acts.", "reasons": "Sulami twice transmits Wasiti's admonition of spiritual elders; Mawardi reports contemplatives' admonitions against sins. {"id": "21:18/q22", "question": "What Fatiha and angel reports occur among these notes?", "turns_on": "Whether the angel prayer anecdote permits angelic recitation or recitation remains a human privilege.", "positions": [{"id": "21:18/q22/p1", "position": "An anecdote suggests angels recite al-Fatiha alone.", "reasons": "A man saw Umar pray at night with only al-Fatiha, then glorify, bow and prostrate; Umar called it the angels' prayer. {"id": "21:18/q23", "question": "What merits are reported for hearing or reciting al-Fatiha?", "turns_on": "These reports describe different acts and rewards.", "positions": [{"id": "21:18/q23/p1", "position": "Hearing its opening or completion earns merit likened to witnessing battle or distribution of spoils.", "reasons": "Abu Qilaba transmits this from the Prophet."}, {"id": "21:18/q23/p2", "position": "Reciting it with another sura before sleep brings an angel companion on waking.", "reasons": "Suyuti reports this Prophetic saying."}]}
{"id": "21:18/q24", "question": "What is reported about al-Fatiha in prayer?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "21:18/q24/p1", "position": "Prayer without al-Fatiha is invalid or deficient; al-Fatiha can substitute for other recitation but nothing substitutes for it.", "reasons": "Suyuti reports the Prophet's 'no prayer' ruling, the Mother of the Quran's unique sufficiency, Abu Hurayra's deficient/deceptive prayer report, and a threefold repetition that prayer without the Mother of the Book is deficient."}]}
{"id": "22:11/q01", "question": "Why say 'from the people' rather than use a pronoun?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "22:11/q01/p1", "position": "The fresh noun evokes the group's instability and vacillation.", "reasons": "Al-Biqāʿī ties the wording to their precarious worship."}]}
{"id": "22:11/q02", "question": "How does the definite class noun in 'from the people' work?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "22:11/q02/p1", "position": "The article can mark a class applicable to each member.", "reasons": "Sībawayh illustrates definite class names through epithets, stars, days, place names and duals. {"id": "22:11/q03", "question": "Who is the conditional worshipper, and what occasion is reported?", "turns_on": "Whether the verse is tied to a particular migrant or incident, a group of conditional converts, hypocrites, or weak converts; Ibn ʿĀshūr objects that concealed disbelief cannot explain reassurance after conversion.", "positions": [{"id": "22:11/q03/p1", "position": "Bedouin or other Arab migrants judged Islam by health, children, animals, harvests, charity and wealth, remaining during prosperity and leaving after misfortune.", "reasons": "Muqātil specifies Asad ibn Khuzayma and Ghaṭafān; reports vary between one newcomer and groups, foals and horses, sons versus daughters or miscarriages, fever, drought and delayed alms. Ibn Kathīr cites Bukhārī for Ibn ʿAbbās's individual report. Ibn ʿĀshūr treats this as evidence for a Medinan occasion; al-Ṭabāṭabāʾ notes two routes. Ibn Jurayj adds nearby villagers; some feared loss of Jewish allies' protection if Muhammad failed. Al-Farrāʾ specifies Banū Asad's move to Medina with their families, their boast about bringing them, and their dependence on alms and safe herds."}, {"id": "22:11/q03/p2", "position": "A Jewish convert suffered loss of sight, wealth and children, asked to leave Islam, and was refused.", "reasons": "Abū Saʿīd's report has the Prophet compare Islam's testing to fire purifying iron, silver and gold; wording also says Islam does not release one. Al-Ālūsī says Ibn Ḥajar weakened the report. Study Quran reports the refining saying without the full identification."}, {"id": "22:11/q03/p3", "position": "Shayba ibn Rabīʿa is identified as the person.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAbbās's version says he accepted Islam before Muhammad's mission and apostatized when revelation began; another account connects conditional belief to requests for wealth, animals and children."}, {"id": "22:11/q03/p4", "position": "The verse concerns hypocrites whose profession depends on outward benefit.", "reasons": "Al-Ḥasan says worship is only on the tongue; Ibn Zayd says worldly ease governs worship. Ibn ʿĀshūr reports ʿAbd Allāh ibn Ubayy among them but objects that concealed unbelief ill fits reassurance after conversion; Jishumī distinguishes weak Muslims who can apostatize from hypocrites who were always unbelievers."}, {"id": "22:11/q03/p5", "position": "Weak or uncertain Muslims, rather than established hypocrites, are described.", "reasons": "Jishumī's distinction is that weak Muslims might actually apostatize; Ibn ʿĀshūr describes entrants neither secure in Islam nor wholly rejecting it, weighing the new faith against old gods."}, {"id": "22:11/q03/p6", "position": "Banū Asad ibn Khuzayma demanded gifts and threatened to return to polytheism if denied.", "reasons": "Jishumī transmits this as another report, distinct in its demand for gifts."}, {"id": "22:11/q03/p7", "position": "Al-Naḍr ibn al-Ḥārith is another named identification.", "reasons": "Al-Qurṭubī lists it among alternatives."}, {"id": "22:11/q03/p8", "position": "ʿUyayna ibn Badr, Aqraʿ ibn Ḥābis and ʿAbbās ibn Mirdās are named.", "reasons": "Elmalılı reports they would accept Muhammad's religion if it brought good and otherwise call it false."}, {"id": "22:11/q03/p9", "position": "The ʿUrayniyyūn exemplify the wavering converts.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr says they migrated, disliked Medina, recovered with charity-camel milk and urine, then killed a shepherd and stole camels before capture and execution; Ibn ʿAṭiyya also invokes them."}]}
{"id": "22:11/q04", "question": "What does worshipping God 'on an edge' mean?", "turns_on": "The literal edge image can point to doubt, one-sided conditional worship, mere outward profession, or a specific inward dependence on reward; several sources explicitly connec

{"id": "22:11/q05", "question": "What does the word ḥarf literally denote here?", "turns_on": "Whether the root image is physical boundary or a transferred sense of mode; Abū al-Fatḥ disputes derivation from inclination.", "positions": [{"id": "22:11/q05/p1", "position": "An edge, side, margin, end or boundary.", "reasons": "Al-Wāḥidī and Jishumī cite the sword's edge and related turning aside; Abū al-Fatḥ derives the root from sharpness or limits and adduces pungent food or plants and distancing; another derivation is inclination from the center. {"id": "22:11/q06", "question": "How should one answer the challenge 'on which letter do you worship'?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "22:11/q06/p1", "position": "One worships God alone without partner.", "reasons": "Muqātil gives this reply to a questioner."}]}
{"id": "22:11/q07", "question": "How is the seven-aḥruf tradition related to the word ḥarf here?", "turns_on": "Whether ḥarf means content aspect, language, or a transmitted reading form, and whether the cited reports are sound.", "positions": [{"id": "22:11/q07/p1", "position": "Seven aḥruf are seven modes or aspects, including kinds of content or divine names, distinct from permitted variant recitations.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAṭiyya describes paths including permission and prohibition; Ubayy's prophetic report permits examples among divine names but not swapping punishment for mercy. Ibn ʿAbd al-Barr calls Ibn Masʿūd's report weak; al-Bayhaqī's disconnected chain is called good though Abū Salama never met Ibn Masʿūd. Ibn ʿAṭiyya says any original name-substitution permission was later abrogated and is now impermissible."}, {"id": "22:11/q07/p2", "position": "The aḥruf mean seven distinct languages.", "reasons": "A reported view takes the number literally as languages; al-Qāḍī Abū Bakr objects that ʿUmar, Ubayy, Hishām and Ibn Masʿūd shared one language yet disputed readings."}, {"id": "22:11/q07/p3", "position": "Every word that has variants must possess seven forms, some unattested.", "reasons": "One group's reasoning is that otherwise the seven-aḥruf hadith would not be fulfilled; missing forms may simply have no transmitted report."}, {"id": "22:11/q07/p4", "position": "It suffices if one or two words have seven forms.", "reasons": "Another group says this fulfills the hadith's wording."}, {"id": "22:11/q07/p5", "position": "Seven aḥruf are seven linguistic modes or vocalic allowances.", "reasons": "Al-Dānī uses ḥarf as a face or aspect, or a part naming the whole reading because a single letter may change. {"id": "22:11/q08", "question": "What do the faʿla noun forms cited alongside this verse indicate?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "22:11/q08/p1", "position": "Faʿla can name a manner or kind of act, and its regular use can name one occurrence; lexical exceptions must be recognized.", "reasons": "Sībawayh distinguishes qatlah and ṭaʿmah for kinds from one event; the direct verbal base supplies the regular single-occurrence form because augmented verbal nouns are not uniformly productive. {"id": "22:11/q09", "question": "What does the good that befalls him comprise?", "turns_on": "Whether 'good' names material circumstances alone or also the convert's inference about religious truth.", "positions": [{"id": "22:11/q09/p1", "position": "Worldly ease: health, livelihood, fertility, wealth, sons and increased livestock.", "reasons": "Mujāhid says prosperity; Qatāda adds crops, comforts and pleasures. {"id": "22:11/q10", "question": "What does being reassured by that good mean?", "turns_on": "Whether the assurance is mere conditional settling or an asserted certainty.", "positions": [{"id": "22:11/q10/p1", "position": "He becomes settled and content in Islam while prosperity continues.", "reasons": "Mujāhid glosses it as becoming established; al-Māwardī says it may strengthen faith or settle him in his position. {"id": "22:11/q12", "question": "Why use 'fitna' for hardship rather than call it evil?", "turns_on": "One explanation concerns moral wording, another the smallness suggested by grammatical form.", "positions": [{"id": "22:11/q12/p1", "position": "Hardship is not inherently evil, and 'fitna' names a burdensome test without moral blame.", "reasons": "Al-Rāzī records Muqātil's question about the contrast with 'good'; Arabic often reserves fitna in this context for what feels hard, although blessings also test. {"id": "22:11/q13", "question": "What does 'turns back on his face' convey?", "turns_on": "Whether the turn refers primarily to apostasy, physical flight or emotional reversal; al-Rāzī addresses how a hypocrite could 'turn back'.", "positions": [{"id": "22:11/q13/p1", "position": "He abandons Islam and returns to disbelief or former idol worship.", "reasons": "Mujāhid, Abū Isḥāq and others gloss apostasy; al-Mubarrad says 'face' may be his former direction. {"id": "22:11/q15", "question": "Which readings of 'lost this world and the next' are reported?", "turns_on": "The variant changes verb to participle and case; the participle may be circumstantial or nominative, with accompanying case differences.", "positions": [{"id": "22:11/q15/p1", "position": "The common reading has the past verb khasira and accusative 'the Hereafter'.", "reasons": "Al-Farrāʾ says it has the same core sense as khāsir; al-Ṭabarī says all regional readers except Ḥumayd al-Aʿraj use it. {"id": "22:11/q16", "question": "What is the loss of this world and the Hereafter?", "turns_on": "The notes differ on whether worldly loss means missed hoped-for goods, actual bereavement or death, legal and social exclusion, or moral waste.", "positions": [{"id": "22:11/q16/p1", "position": "He misses the worldly benefit he sought and loses afterlife reward through unbelief or apostasy.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabarī says uncertain worship fails to secure worldly aims and leads to Fire; Yahyā says his cherished worldly life passes and he has no share beyond. Al-Wāḥidī, Ibn Kathīr and Study Quran connect missed goods to rejection of faith. Kashifī adds destruction of deeds.
